audioScript:
Good morning, Midya. It's Friday, September eighteenth, twenty twenty-six. It's a quieter news cycle than we've had all week, so today I'm going deep on a handful of stories that genuinely matter to your work rather than skating across a dozen that don't.

Let's start with AI, because two stories today land squarely in the middle of your thesis about where marketing operations are heading — and one of them is almost tailor-made for a contrarian post.

The first is a small item out of India that's bigger than it looks. A media agency called Celewish has introduced what it's branding an 'AI virtual CMO' — a named AI persona, Maira Vardhan, positioned to lead celebrity and influencer marketing. Now, on its face this is a publicity stunt, and you should treat it as one. But it's a very revealing stunt. Because the reason it works as marketing is that a chunk of the industry genuinely believes, or wants to believe, that senior marketing judgment can be abstracted into a persona and sold as a service. And that's the exact fault line I'd want you standing on publicly. The strong take here isn't 'AI can't do marketing' — that's the lazy contrarian position and it's already wrong at the execution layer. The sharp take is about accountability. A chief marketing officer is not a content engine. A CMO owns tradeoffs, owns brand risk, owns the decision about what not to do, and owns the consequences when a campaign misfires. You cannot delegate accountability to a persona, and the moment a brand pretends it has, it's created a governance vacuum. That's your lane. There's a genuinely good piece of thought leadership in contrasting the 'AI virtual CMO' theatre against what real AI augmentation of a marketing function actually looks like — where AI compresses the production and analysis layers so that human strategists spend more time on judgment, not less. I'd write that one.

The second AI story is the substance behind the theatre. A company called Datasea reported it has signed five agreements worth up to roughly eighty-nine million US dollars in annualized service volume for what it calls AI agent digital-marketing services. Strip away the press-release gloss and the signal is this: agentic AI in marketing is moving from pilot to production, and it's being contracted at real scale. This is the thing to watch, because it changes the nature of the conversation you'll be having with clients within a year. When agents are executing campaigns semi-autonomously — planning, buying, optimizing — the questions that matter stop being 'can it do the work' and become 'who owns the measurement, who's accountable for brand safety, and where does the data live.' That last one is your public-institution governance lens exactly. If a Canadian university or a public-sector client deploys agentic marketing, FIPPA and BC data residency don't get suspended because the operator is an algorithm. There's a productizable audit checklist in here: before you let an AI agent run marketing operations, what are the ten questions you must be able to answer about data flow, measurement integrity, and human override? That's a framework you could publish and use as a sales artifact at the same time.

Staying close to marketing craft, two campaigns worth a moment. The first is Coleman, the outdoor brand, which built a social and ecommerce campaign around a deliberately fake AI product — an 'AI' lazy river — and turned it into a genuine engagement win. I like this one because it's the counter-melody to the Datasea story. Coleman read the room correctly: a meaningful slice of the audience is fatigued by earnest AI announcements, and the brand converted that fatigue into affection by being in on the joke. The lesson for any marketer is that cultural sentiment reading still beats trend-chasing. You don't win by being the loudest adopter of a technology; you win by understanding how your audience actually feels about it. That's a nuance a lot of AI-first marketing shops are missing right now.

The second is Wonderful Pistachios, which built its first NIL — name, image, likeness — athlete roster into a social campaign called 'Don't Hold Back All-Stars,' featuring seven rising college athletes and borrowing openly from Nike's playbook. I flag this less for the creative and more for the structural signal: NIL talent is now a mainstream brand-marketing channel, and it sits right at the intersection of your two lanes — consumer brand marketing and higher education. College athletes are becoming media properties, and institutions that understand how to co-market with their own student-athletes have a brand asset most of them are underusing. If you're ever building enrollment-brand strategy for a Canadian institution, the NIL model — even in its more constrained Canadian form — is a useful reference for how student stories become recruitment gravity.

Now to higher education and international students, where the demand picture keeps getting clearer, and the message is consistent across every destination.

Start with the UK. New Home Office data shows sponsored study-visa applications fell to their lowest August level since twenty twenty-two. August matters enormously in that cycle — it accounts for at least a quarter of all applications lodged in a year — so a weak August isn't noise, it's a trend confirmation. Pair that with a story out of Nigeria reporting that Canadian visa and study-permit processing times are climbing for Nigerian applicants, one of Canada's larger source markets, and you get a coherent picture: the international recruitment funnel is getting harder everywhere at once. Softening demand in the UK, more friction in Canada's processing pipeline, and — as we covered earlier this week — Australia tightening rules on student dependants and visa hopping. Every major destination is simultaneously less accessible or less attractive than it was two years ago.

Here's why this matters for your practice specifically. When the total pool shrinks and the friction rises, the premium shifts to conversion efficiency. The institutions that survive this environment are the ones that can turn a smaller number of qualified prospects into enrolled students without leaking them at every stage of a slow, confusing funnel. That is a marketing and operations problem before it's a policy problem — and it's precisely the problem you sell into. When you talk to Canadian institutions this fall, the framing I'd lead with is: policy has capped your top of funnel, so your only growth lever left is conversion, and conversion is where AI-assisted, well-governed marketing operations actually earn their keep. The schools that keep spending on brand awareness while their conversion machinery leaks are optimizing the wrong thing.

There's also a softer, strategic piece from ICEF asking how the sector should tell the story of international education. It gets at the tension between federal immigration policy and the regional towns and campuses that depend on international students economically. It's a narrative problem the sector keeps failing to solve — it lets itself be framed as a housing-and-immigration liability instead of an economic and cultural asset. There's genuine thought-leadership terrain here about reframing the value story, and it's adjacent to the brand work you do.

On real estate, one story from California that's worth watching precisely because it's a preview of a BC fight. California's SB 79 upzoning law — which forces higher density near transit — is now drawing lawsuits. Plaintiffs argue the density rules were applied too narrowly, that sidewalk-gap and train-frequency criteria were used to illegally disqualify parcels that should have qualified for upzoning. Why does a San Diego zoning suit belong in your briefing? Because transit-oriented upzoning is exactly the policy lever BC municipalities are now pulling, and the legal mechanics of how you define 'transit-adjacent' and who gets to litigate the boundaries are going to be fought here too. For your husband's brokerage and for the commercial investment-sales side of your practice, the value of a parcel increasingly turns on these definitional fights. The lesson is that upzoning entitlements aren't settled the day the law passes — they're settled parcel by parcel in the disputes that follow, and that's where value gets created and destroyed.

A few things from the wider world you should have in your peripheral vision as a senior leader.

The headline of the day: Warren Buffett is stepping down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway at ninety-six, handing the role to his son Howard, less than a year after he gave up the CEO seat. This is the formal close of an era in capital allocation and corporate stewardship. Whatever you think of Berkshire's specific bets, Buffett's core discipline — long time horizons, clarity about your circle of competence, and a refusal to confuse activity with progress — is exactly the mindset worth carrying into your own consulting build-out. As you productize your methodologies through twenty twenty-six and twenty-seven, the temptation is always to chase every shiny AI development. The Buffett discipline is the antidote: know what you're actually expert in, and compound in that lane.

Second, oil. J.P. Morgan analysts made an unusually honest admission — they've dropped their baseline forecast for oil because they no longer know how to model the endgame around the Strait of Hormuz and the Iran conflict. The takeaway isn't a specific price prediction; it's that energy input costs are entering a prolonged period of genuine uncertainty, and that uncertainty flows into everything from transportation to construction to the broader inflation picture that shapes interest rates and, downstream, the real estate market you watch.

And more soberly, a bombing at a mosque next to a police building in Peshawar, in northwestern Pakistan, killed at least fifteen people and wounded dozens — part of a continuing wave of attacks on security infrastructure in the region. Worth being aware of as a marker of ongoing instability in South Asia, a region that, incidentally, is central to the international-student flows we just discussed.

On the health front, one piece from STAT News that's genuinely practical. A physician writes that doctors should treat 'Asian glow' — the facial flushing many people of East Asian descent experience when drinking — as a real medical signal, not a cosmetic quirk. The flushing is tied to a variant of the ALDH2 gene that impairs the body's ability to clear acetaldehyde, a carcinogenic byproduct of alcohol metabolism. The consequence is that people who flush and continue to drink carry a meaningfully elevated risk of certain cancers, particularly esophageal cancer. The actionable point is simple: if you or anyone in your family flushes when drinking, that's a body telling you something about how it processes alcohol, and it's worth a real conversation rather than a shrug. It's a rare health story that translates directly into a decision you can actually make.

Finally, two quick local-and-regional notes. First, the emergency department in Merritt is closing for most of today. It's the familiar and frustrating rural-BC ER staffing story, but it's a practical flag if you or family are travelling the Coquihalla corridor or relying on interior health services this weekend — know where the nearest open ER is before you need it. And second, a more forward-looking one: a new satellite-and-machine-learning system is being developed to give earlier warnings for flash floods, the kind that strike rural communities with almost no lead time. Given BC's atmospheric-river and flooding exposure, this is exactly the sort of AI-for-public-safety application worth tracking — and, frankly, it's a cleaner example of AI doing something unambiguously good than most of what dominates the discourse.

That's your Friday, Midya. If you do one thing with today's briefing, let it be the AI-virtual-CMO angle — it's the rare story that lets you stake out a smart, defensible position that flatters neither the hype nor the reflexive skepticism, and it points straight at your governance-and-accountability strength. Everything else this week has been telling the same story: AI is moving into the operating core of marketing while the international-student funnel keeps narrowing, and both of those trends make the disciplined, well-governed advisor more valuable, not less. Have a good weekend up on the mountain — I'll be back Monday.
